text: Gold exists. But a table existing isn't the same claim as a table being correct. This lesson validates that the three layers you've built actually agree with each other.

PySpark will happily finish a job with a wrong countDistinct, a bad filter, or a join that silently multiplied rows, and never raise an exception. The table gets written, the job shows success, and the numbers are simply wrong. So this step counts rows at every layer — bronze, silver, gold — plus the number of distinct sale dates in Silver — and prints all four numbers out before trusting any of them.

Then two assertions turn those counts into real checks. First: silver count can never be greater than bronze count, because every operation between them only removes rows — deduplication and null filtering — there's no step that could add rows. Second: gold count must exactly equal the distinct date count in Silver, because Gold's entire grain, fixed back in lesson two, is one row per calendar day.

These aren't arbitrary rules. If lesson four's dedup key had been wrong, or lesson five's group by had accidentally included an extra column alongside sale date, these assertions would fail immediately, with a clear reason — instead of quietly shipping a slightly wrong number to the Store Operations lead, who has no way to catch that just by glancing at a chart.

This isn't a full data quality suite — it doesn't check whether the dollar amount itself looks reasonable, or whether a day is missing entirely. But it's the minimum habit: confirm your layers agree with each other before anything downstream trusts them. Next lesson, you'll turn this notebook from something you run by hand into a pipeline that runs itself, every day.
